title: 11 Vintage Christmas Decorations EVERYONE Threw Away (Bring Them BACK)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, last week my granddaughter showed me a picture of a Christmas ornament in a fancy catalog. A little glass bird with a feather tail. Forty dollars. And I laughed so hard I had to sit down, because I have six of them in a shoebox in my attic. My mother bought them at the five and dime in nineteen fifty-one for a dime apiece.
scenes.caption: FORTY DOLLARS

scenes.text: So tonight I'm giving you eleven vintage Christmas decorations that everybody threw away, and that the stores are now selling back to you for a fortune. For every one, I'll tell you how we used them, and how to get the look for almost nothing. And stay with me, because number eleven is the one I'd save if my house was on fire.
scenes.caption: ELEVEN TO BRING BACK

scenes.text: Number one. The glass clip-on birds. Little glass birds with spun glass tails, clipped right onto the branches with a tiny metal clip, so they look like they just landed on the tree. Every house on Elm Street had a few. You can still find them at antique malls and estate sales for a couple of dollars, if you get there before the catalog people do.
scenes.query: clip on glass bird Christmas tree
scenes.caption: THEY JUST LANDED

scenes.text: Number two. Bubble lights. Tall little candle-shaped lights filled with colored liquid, and when they warmed up, the liquid bubbled. Danny and I lay on the rug under the tree and waited for each one to start bubbling. We made bets on which would go first. They still make them, honey, and ten of them on a tree make the whole room feel like nineteen fifty-five.
scenes.caption: WE MADE BETS

scenes.text: Number three. Real tinsel, hung one strand at a time. Not thrown in clumps, sweetheart. My mother made us hang it one strand at a time, so it hung straight down like icicles. It took the whole evening. And on New Year's Day she took it all off, strand by strand, and laid it in a shoebox for next year. Nothing was thrown away in our house.
scenes.caption: ONE STRAND AT A TIME

scenes.text: Number four. The aluminum tree, with the color wheel. In nineteen sixty, my aunt in Cleveland got a silver aluminum tree, and a lamp on the floor with a wheel of colored plastic that turned slowly, so the tree went red, then blue, then green, then gold. My mother thought it was the ugliest thing she'd ever seen. Danny and I thought it was the future.
scenes.caption: IT WAS THE FUTURE

scenes.text: Number five. Plaid. Red tartan ribbon on the wreath, a plaid blanket folded on the couch, a plaid bow on every present. Plaid is all over the magazines this year, and it was all over my mother's house in nineteen fifty-four. She bought one bolt of red plaid ribbon and used it for ten years, ironing it flat every January.
scenes.caption: ONE BOLT FOR TEN YEARS

scenes.text: To bring plaid back without spending much, honey, pick one plaid and repeat it. A plaid ribbon on the wreath, the same plaid on the stair rail, and a plaid scarf tied around a jar candle. Go to the thrift store for an old wool plaid skirt or blanket, cut it into strips, and you've got enough ribbon for the whole house. Three places, one plaid, and it looks like a magazine.
scenes.caption: ONE PLAID, THREE PLACES

scenes.text: Number six. Felt ornaments, made by hand. My mother cut little stockings, mittens and stars out of felt squares from the dime store, ten cents a square, and we sewed them with big stitches and glued on sequins. The children's hands made them crooked, and that was the beauty of it. Get a pack of felt and an evening, and you'll have a tree full of ornaments with your family's fingerprints on them.
scenes.caption: YOUR FAMILY'S FINGERPRINTS

scenes.text: If this is bringing back memories, honey, tap the like button for me. It helps Grandma more than you know, and it tells me to keep going. In a minute I'll tell you the decoration my mother made every year out of things we'd normally throw in the trash.
scenes.caption: TAP THE LIKE BUTTON

scenes.text: Number seven. Popcorn and cranberry garland. My mother popped a big pot of popcorn, left it out overnight so it got a little stale, because fresh popcorn breaks on the needle. Then we sat at the kitchen table with needles and heavy thread and strung popcorn and cranberries. Three popcorns, one cranberry. Danny ate more than he strung.
scenes.caption: THREE POPCORNS, ONE CRANBERRY

scenes.text: And when Christmas was over, we hung the garland outside on the bushes for the birds. The cardinals came first, then the chickadees. It's the only Christmas decoration I know that gets a second life. And here's the decoration made from trash I promised you. Paper chains. Strips cut from old wrapping paper, the Sunday comics, and Christmas cards, glued in loops.
scenes.caption: A SECOND LIFE

scenes.text: We started the paper chain on the first of December with twenty-four loops, and every night after supper one of us tore off one loop. When the chain was gone, it was Christmas Eve. It was our Advent calendar, and it cost nothing. My great-grandchildren make one every year now, and they fight over whose turn it is to tear.
scenes.caption: WHOSE TURN TO TEAR

scenes.text: Number eight. Candles in every window. Electric candles, one in each front window, with the orange bulb shaped like a flame. In the fifties, you could walk down any street in Mansfield and see every house with a candle in every window. It was a way of saying welcome. Now people put up laser projectors. I'll take my candles.
scenes.caption: A WAY OF SAYING WELCOME
scenes.chapter: 5. Window candles and the ceramic tree

scenes.text: And here's how to do the window candles cheap today. The battery candles with a timer, a few dollars each at the hardware store. Set them to come on at dusk and go off at eleven, and you never have to touch them again. Put one in every front window, upstairs and down. From the street, your house will look exactly like Elm Street in nineteen fifty-five.
scenes.caption: COME ON AT DUSK

scenes.text: Number nine. The ceramic Christmas tree. A little green ceramic tree with tiny colored plastic bulbs that lit up from a light bulb inside. In the seventies, every grandmother in America made one in a ceramics class at the church basement. Mine is on my kitchen table right now. Today they sell for a hundred dollars and more at the antique shops. Check your mother's attic.
scenes.caption: CHECK YOUR MOTHER'S ATTIC

scenes.text: So far, glass birds, bubble lights, tinsel, the aluminum tree, plaid, felt, popcorn garland, window candles, and the ceramic tree. Number ten. Christmas cards on display. My mother strung a red ribbon across the doorway to the living room and hung every card we received with a clothespin. By Christmas, the doorway was covered. You could read the whole year of our family and friends on that ribbon.
scenes.caption: A YEAR ON A RIBBON

scenes.text: And now number eleven, the one I'd save if my house was on fire. The nativity set. Ours was cardboard and painted plaster, from nineteen forty-seven, with a wooden stable my father built out of an apple crate. Mary has a chipped nose from when Danny dropped her in nineteen fifty-two. The baby went in the manger only on Christmas morning, not one day before.
scenes.caption: NOT ONE DAY BEFORE

scenes.text: My mother's rule was that the youngest child put the baby in the manger on Christmas morning, before anybody opened a present. Then the wise men moved a little closer every day until the sixth of January. I still do it. My great-granddaughter put the baby in the manger last year, and she whispered, welcome home. I'm still not over it.
scenes.caption: WELCOME HOME

scenes.text: Now, how to get the vintage look without paying catalog prices. Go to estate sales in December, honey. Families clear out their grandparents' houses, and boxes of glass ornaments go for five dollars. Check the thrift stores the week after Christmas. And ask your own family. There's a box in somebody's attic or basement with your grandmother's ornaments in it, and nobody has opened it in twenty years.
scenes.query: box of vintage ornaments estate sale
scenes.caption: A BOX IN SOMEBODY'S ATTIC

scenes.text: And mix them, don't match. The old trees were never perfect. A glass bird next to a felt mitten next to a ball with the paint worn off. That's what makes it look real, and warm, and yours. A tree that looks like it came out of a box looks cheap. A tree that looks like it came out of a life looks like a treasure.
scenes.caption: OUT OF A LIFE

scenes.text: And handle the old glass ornaments gently. They're thin as an eggshell. Hang them by the cap, not the hook, and keep them high, out of reach of the cat and the toddlers. When you pack them away, wrap each one in tissue paper, and store them in an egg carton or a box with dividers. That's how mine have lasted seventy-five years.
scenes.caption: THIN AS AN EGGSHELL

scenes.text: So one more time. Glass birds, bubble lights, real tinsel one strand at a time, the aluminum tree, plaid ribbon, felt ornaments, popcorn and cranberry garland, the paper chain, candles in the windows, the ceramic tree, cards on a ribbon, and the nativity. Every one of them cost almost nothing, and every one of them is worth more than anything in that catalog.
scenes.query: vintage Christmas tree warm living room
scenes.caption: WORTH MORE THAN THE CATALOG

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. Which one did your family have? I bet half of you had the aluminum tree. If you want more, the whole playlist of Grandma's Christmas tips is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.caption: WHICH ONE DID YOU HAVE?
